en: The Sūtra on Contemplating the Body, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. This...
Then the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"This body possesses skin, flesh, marrow, blood, and fat, and is filled with excrement and urine; when you look upon this body, what do you see as beautiful?"
There are always nine apertures with foul diseases;
it is constantly impure and flows perpetually—this should be sufficient cause for shame.
One is always joined with enemies until old age and death.
It is likewise accompanied by illness; why do you not loathe it?
The body must inevitably fall and must inevitably decay, until it is cast upon the ground as a corpse, no longer of use, and devoured by foxes and wolves—why do you feel no shame at seeing this?
Who says there is lust?
As the Buddha said:
"A small amount of what is agreeable leads to great transgression; observe this within your own mind."
It is like a butcher’s block or a slaughterbench for a heap of bones;
it is like a blazing fire;
it is like a whirlpool of poisonous pain. Yet the foolish person delights in it, unaware of their own joy.
Why do you not fear the net?
Greed and lust arise from delusion; people seek wealth, grain, gold, silver, oxen, horses, slaves, and servants for the sake of their lives.
Yet life exists only in the space between breaths; one's original life is itself brief, with a maximum lifespan of barely over a hundred years.
Furthermore, there is the suffering of association.
Contemplating this, who could find it acceptable?
"As time passes, life gradually diminishes; the days of one's lifespan come to an end."
Like a swift river, like the waning of the sun and moon, life passes away with such speed; once a person's life has departed, it does not return, and thus it cannot be recovered.
When a person dies, their life-force departs; even if they possess vast wealth and can obtain every rare object in the world, at the moment of death, none of these things can bring them joy;
nor can they cause aversion, nor can they bring delight.
Furthermore, one should not delight in the state of nirvana without remainder;
rather, one should simply perform wholesome deeds oneself.
Whatever wholesome deeds one performs are what ought to be done spontaneously.
If one knows that death is inevitable, what joy can there be?
"A person may fall into lust even if they live a long life;
yet even if they depart, death is certain."
For what reason is there attachment to pleasure? Why is this so?
Because one does not contemplate inner stillness, but instead experiences delight with the utmost intensity of mind.
When a child has died, one weeps for no more than ten days; after those ten days have passed, one gradually forgets it.
It is the same with a beloved wife!
It is the same for one's household, kinsmen, and acquaintances!

"By toiling and enduring hardship to acquire wealth and property, and by adorning one's own body and life with finery, when a person dies, they abandon all possessions; the body lies stiff upon the ground, sinking into the earth, departing as mere aggregates (*skandha*). Yet, birth follows as the person receives a new form.

It is like seeing the fruit of a tree already formed: thus it is that the human mind falls into existence. Among all the fruits and goods in the world, even if one person were to obtain them all, they would not be enough for themselves; if one obtains but a single portion, how could one ever be satisfied? There is no end to it."
If one pervades the thirty-five joys with self-joy, what benefit would there be?

When a person encounters suffering, they seek out the mind of one who is undergoing punishment; they consider this a pleasure and believe it to be beneficial. Yet, they do not wish to undergo tranquility, seeking instead to inflict poison and thorns upon themselves; whether it be little or much, it is the same!
It is the same whether it is much or little!
Just as a disease is painful regardless of whether it is great or small;
for example, it is like a bone without flesh that a dog will gnaw upon without ever being satiated.
Such habitual tendencies toward desire are likewise difficult to overcome; once acquired, one should stand in great fear of them.
These habits do not endure for long, yet people fall into evil because of them.
It is like a person who sees a dream: once they have woken up, it can no longer be obtained. So too is it with lustful craving.
Theatrical performances are like dreams; though they appear to have pleasure, they are like a black snare or baited hook.

They are like the fruit of a tree, where the substance is meager while the flavor is abundant; they increase delusion and bondage, serving as the root of evil deeds, and are therefore never employed by the Daoists.
"This person shall abandon the pleasures of the heavens, as well as the celestial trees of exquisite color;
they shall dwell in magnificent and beautiful parks and gardens,
and shall obtain celestial jade maidens."
Having already attained the status of gods and humans, they do not grow weary of the five pleasures of the heavens; how then could they now grow weary of the pleasures of the human world?
"To take up two hundred days' worth of bones, with one hundred and twenty segments bound together by sinews;
to have nine orifices constantly leaking;"
It constitutes sixty-three kinds;
it is the limit of a hundred maladies;
it is the confluence of flesh and blood.
For the sake of producing skin;
for the sake of enduring cold, heat, and wind;
for the sake of excrement and urine; and for the sake of the thousands of worms—all these arise from the body, and within it there are also a thousand orifices.
There are also severe cases where, having harmed others for the sake of one's own kin, impurity issues forth from them;
it issues as nasal mucus from the nostrils,
or as saliva and spittle from the mouth.
Sweat flows from the armpits;
excrement and urine emerge from the lower orifices—all these issues issue forth from the body with great intensity.
The corpses within the charnel grounds are truly loathsome and terrible.

In the loathsome places behind one's dwelling, the impurities of the body are likewise: they are the seeds of impurity; from the very beginning, they are like gold smeared upon other objects, or like clothing perfumed with fragrances, powders, unguents, red cotton-wool, indigo, and collyrium;
yet the deluded person perceives them as such and their mind becomes distracted.
"It is like a painted jar, red as if covered with grass in a pit; though people embrace it with love, they will later feel regret.
When the bhikṣu heard this sutra, he prostrated and received it; such is the teaching of the Way.
The Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Body (Kāyagatāsati-sutta)
